answer.exemplar: A test can only compute the probability of the observed data under some stated assumption, so one of the two claims has to play the role of the assumption and the other the role of what is being argued for. Putting the null in the assumption slot makes the reasoning a contradiction: take the effect to be absent, ask how often results this extreme would arise, and if that is rare the assumption has been ruled out and the burden falls on the claim that wanted to overturn it. A test that assumed the alternative instead would be computing the tail probability of the very thing it was meant to test, which is why the convention is not arbitrary. Rejection also leaves the alternative merely standing rather than proved, so the default can be ruled out without its rival being established.

Saying the null is conventional is not enough, since the reader cannot tell whether the convention has a reason. The closing point matters too, because rejection rules the default out without establishing its rival.
questions.hint: Ask which assumption the tail probability is being computed under.

answer.exemplar: The interval is built from a sample, so its meaning attaches to the method rather than to the parameter. Before any data arrive, the procedure that produces such intervals will cover the true value 95 times in 100, and miss it 5 times in 100, and that long-run coverage is the only thing the 95 percent describes. Once a specific interval has been computed the parameter is fixed, so it is simply inside or outside, with no probability left to attach to which. A model answer must make that switch from procedure to realised interval explicit, and must reject the reading that 95 percent of the parameter lies within the interval, which quietly treats a fixed quantity as if it were random and so assigns it a distribution it does not have.

questions.explanation: A model answer must separate the long-run property of the method from the fixed status of the parameter, since that is the whole content of the interval and the usual misreading collapses the two. A 95 percent figure says nothing about where the parameter sits, only about how often the method catches it. Rejecting the parameter-as-random reading is what shows the distinction was understood rather than merely quoted.
questions.hint: Ask whether the randomness lies in the method or in the parameter itself.
questions.learningObjective: explain the meaning of a confidence interval

answer.exemplar: A correlation coefficient is computed from co-variation in the observed data and carries no information about direction of influence, because several distinct mechanisms all produce co-variation. A third variable can drive both, so the pair moves together with neither causing the other, and a reversed order of measurement does the same thing when one quantity simply follows the other in time. The association may also hold only where the data were gathered, which makes the coefficient a summary of that sample rather than a law about the world. A model answer must name at least the confounding case and the reversed-direction case, since a bare assertion that correlation is not causation teaches nothing about why, and it should close by naming a design, such as a controlled manipulation or a natural experiment, that would settle the question.

questions.explanation: A model answer must name the mechanisms, above all a shared third variable and a reversed direction, because without them the claim is a slogan rather than an argument. A coefficient can be arbitrarily large and still be produced by a confounder. Closing with a design that would settle the question turns the objection into something actionable rather than merely defensive.
questions.hint: Name two different mechanisms that both produce a high coefficient.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a correlation does not establish a causal direction

answer.exemplar: A series recorded over time mixes several kinds of movement. The trend is the slow direction in which the level drifts over the long run, the seasonal component is a pattern that repeats on a fixed cycle such as a week or a year, and the irregular part is whatever remains once those two are taken out, being the noise together with any one-off disruption. Separating them matters because the three call for different responses: a trend usually reflects something structural in the system, a seasonal pattern is often an artefact of how the data happened to be collected, and the irregular part is mostly what a forecast should decline to predict. A model answer must name all three components, since naming only trend and season leaves the reader with nowhere to put the remainder, and must give at least one reason the split matters beyond description.

questions.explanation: A model answer must name all three components, because a decomposition with only trend and seasonality leaves the reader with nowhere to put what is left over. The usefulness argument is the part usually skipped, and it is what makes decomposition a method rather than a description. Connecting seasonality to a collection artefact is a good concrete instance of the different responses the three components invite.
questions.hint: Name the long-run movement, the repeating cycle and the remainder.
questions.learningObjective: explain the components a time series separates into

questions.explanation: Conditioning on card use leaves the 60 card users, and 12 of those own a bicycle, so the probability is 12 over 60, which is 0.2. Independence has to be tested with the product of the marginals instead: 0.3 times 0.6 is 0.18, while the shared share is 0.12, and since those differ the two are not independent. Bicycle owners in fact under-use the card, because 0.12 falls short of the 0.18 the marginals alone would predict.
questions.hint: Conditioning divides by the conditioning group; independence compares with the product.

questions.explanation: The standard error is the standard deviation over the square root of the sample size, and the square root of 49 is 7, so 21 over 7 is 3. An interval reaching one standard error either side of the mean runs from 61 to 67, which is 6 wide, because a reach of 3 at each of the two ends makes 6 in total. The tempting slip is to quote the 3 as the width, but an interval has two sides and the margin applies to each.

Extrapolating from (2, 6) out to x equal to 8 is a run of 6, so the rise is 1.5 times 6, which is 9, and the prediction is 6 plus 9, giving 15. questions.explanation: Both row totals and both column totals are 40 out of 80, so independence expects 40 times 40 over 80 in every cell, which is 20. Each observed count differs from 20 by 10, so each cell contributes 100 over 20, which is 5, and there are four cells, making the statistic 20. Using a single cell alone, as the second option does, discards three quarters of the evidence against independence.
